## Metric Spaces

A metric is a generalisation of the concept of distance between points of a set.
Metric spaces are the setting in which convergence, continuity and completeness
make sense without any algebraic structure. They sit between
[[normed-space|normed spaces]] (a metric from a norm) and general
[[topology|topological spaces]] (open sets without a metric).

:::{.definition data-title="Metric Space"}

A **metric** on a set $X$ is a function $d:X\times X\to[0,\infty)$ such that for
all $x,y,z\in X$:

1. $d(x,y)=0$ if and only if $x=y$;
2. $d(x,y)=d(y,x)$ (symmetry);
3. $d(x,z)\leq d(x,y)+d(y,z)$ (triangle inequality).

The pair $(X,d)$ is a **metric space**.

:::

:::{.example data-title="Examples of Metrics"}

- **Euclidean:** $d(x,y)=\lvert x-y\rvert$ on $\mathbb{R}$, and
  $d(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert_2$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. More generally any
  [[normed-space|norm]] gives a metric $d(x,y)=\lVert x-y\rVert$.
- **Discrete:** $d(x,y)=1$ if $x\neq y$ and $0$ otherwise, on any set $X$.
- **Function spaces:** on $C([0,1])$,
  $d_\infty(f,g)=\sup_{x\in[0,1]}\lvert f(x)-g(x)\rvert$ and
  $d_1(f,g)=\int_0^1\lvert f(x)-g(x)\rvert\,dx$. For $d_1$, the condition
  $d_1(f,g)=0\implies f=g$ uses continuity: a nonzero continuous function has a
  positive integral. (On merely integrable functions $d_1$ is only a
  pseudometric.)
- **Extended reals:** $\overline{\mathbb{R}}=\mathbb{R}\cup\{\pm\infty\}$ with
  $d(x,y)=\lvert\varphi(x)-\varphi(y)\rvert$, where
  $\varphi(x)=\frac{x}{1+\lvert x\rvert}$ and $\varphi(\pm\infty)=\pm1$. This is a
  metric because $\varphi$ is injective, and it makes $\varphi$ an isometry onto
  $[-1,1]$. Hence $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is a compact metric space.

:::

## Open and Closed Sets

:::{.definition data-title="Open Ball, Open Set, Closed Set"}

The **open ball** of radius $\epsilon>0$ about $x\in X$ is
$B_\epsilon(x)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)<\epsilon\}$, and the **closed ball** is
$\bar B_\epsilon(x)=\{y\in X:d(x,y)\leq\epsilon\}$. A set $A\subseteq X$ is
**open** if for every $x\in A$ there is $\epsilon>0$ with $B_\epsilon(x)\subseteq A$.
A set is **closed** if its complement is open.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Topology of a Metric Space"}

In a metric space $(X,d)$:

1. Open balls are open.
2. $\emptyset$ and $X$ are open, arbitrary unions of open sets are open, and
   finite intersections of open sets are open.
3. Dually, $\emptyset$ and $X$ are closed, arbitrary intersections of closed
   sets are closed, and finite unions of closed sets are closed.

:::

:::{.proof}
(1) If $y\in B_\epsilon(x)$ let $\delta=\epsilon-d(x,y)>0$. For
$z\in B_\delta(y)$ the triangle inequality gives
$d(x,z)\leq d(x,y)+d(y,z)<\epsilon$, so $B_\delta(y)\subseteq B_\epsilon(x)$.

(2) A point in a union lies in one of the sets, hence has a ball inside it. For
$x\in U_1\cap\cdots\cap U_n$ choose $\epsilon_i$ with $B_{\epsilon_i}(x)\subseteq U_i$
and take $\epsilon=\min_i\epsilon_i>0$. The finite requirement is needed: in
$\mathbb{R}$, $\bigcap_n(-\tfrac1n,\tfrac1n)=\{0\}$ is not open.

(3) follows from (2) by taking complements ([[set-theory-fundamentals#Algebra of Sets|De Morgan]]).
:::

Open sets are exactly what a [[topology]] axiomatises: a collection of sets
closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. A set can be both open
and closed (such as $\emptyset$ and $X$) or neither (such as $[0,1)$ in
$\mathbb{R}$). The countable intersections of open sets ($G_\delta$) and
countable unions of closed sets ($F_\sigma$) feed into the
[[borel-measure|Borel σ-algebra]].

## Convergence and Continuity

:::{.definition data-title="Convergence in a Metric Space"}

A sequence $\{x_n\}$ in $(X,d)$ **converges** to $x\in X$, written $x_n\to x$, if
$d(x_n,x)\to0$, that is, for every $\epsilon>0$ there is $N$ with
$d(x_n,x)<\epsilon$ for all $n\geq N$. See [[sequence-convergence]] for the real
case.

:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Closed Sets and Sequences"}

$A\subseteq X$ is closed if and only if whenever $x_n\in A$ and $x_n\to x\in X$,
we have $x\in A$.

:::

:::{.proof}
($\Rightarrow$) Suppose $A$ is closed, $x_n\in A$, $x_n\to x$ and $x\notin A$.
Since $A^c$ is open there is $\epsilon>0$ with $B_\epsilon(x)\subseteq A^c$, but
$x_n\in B_\epsilon(x)$ for large $n$, contradicting $x_n\in A$.
($\Leftarrow$) Suppose $A$ is not closed, so $A^c$ is not open: there is
$x\in A^c$ with $B_{1/n}(x)\cap A\neq\emptyset$ for every $n$. Choosing
$x_n\in B_{1/n}(x)\cap A$ gives $x_n\to x$ with $x\notin A$.
:::

:::{.theorem data-title="Continuity"}

For $f:(X,d_X)\to(Y,d_Y)$ and $x_0\in X$ the following are equivalent:

1. **$\epsilon$-$\delta$:** for all $\epsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ with
   $d_X(x,x_0)<\delta\implies d_Y(f(x),f(x_0))<\epsilon$.
2. **Sequential:** $x_n\to x_0$ implies $f(x_n)\to f(x_0)$.

Moreover $f$ is continuous at every point if and only if $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in
$X$ for every open $V\subseteq Y$.

:::

:::{.proof}
(1)$\Rightarrow$(2): given $\epsilon$ take $\delta$ from (1), then
$d_X(x_n,x_0)<\delta$ for large $n$ gives $d_Y(f(x_n),f(x_0))<\epsilon$.
(2)$\Rightarrow$(1): if (1) fails there is $\epsilon>0$ such that for every $n$ some
$x_n$ has $d_X(x_n,x_0)<1/n$ but $d_Y(f(x_n),f(x_0))\geq\epsilon$, contradicting (2).

For the last claim, if $f$ is $\epsilon$-$\delta$ continuous and $V$ is open, take
$x_0\in f^{-1}(V)$ and $\epsilon$ with $B_\epsilon(f(x_0))\subseteq V$; then
$B_\delta(x_0)\subseteq f^{-1}(V)$. Conversely, apply the open-preimage condition
to $V=B_\epsilon(f(x_0))$ to get an open set containing $x_0$, hence a ball
$B_\delta(x_0)$ inside it.
:::

The open-preimage formulation is the one that survives in topology and in
[[measure-spaces|measure theory]], where a function is *measurable* when preimages
of open (Borel) sets are measurable, see [[set-functions]]. A bijection $f$ such
that $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are continuous is a **homeomorphism**.

## Completeness and Compactness

:::{.definition data-title="Cauchy Sequence & Complete Space"}

A sequence $\{x_n\}$ is **Cauchy** if for all $\epsilon>0$ there is $N$ with
$d(x_n,x_m)<\epsilon$ for all $n,m\geq N$. A metric space is **complete** if every
Cauchy sequence converges to a point of the space.

:::

Every convergent sequence is Cauchy (see [[cauchy-sequence]]), but the converse
depends on the space. $\mathbb{R}$ is complete while $\mathbb{Q}$ is not (a
rational sequence can converge to $\sqrt2$). See [[completeness]].

:::{.example data-title="$(C([0,1]),d_\infty)$ is complete but $(C([0,1]),d_1)$ is not"}

$C([0,1])$ with $d_\infty$ is complete, as uniform limits of continuous functions
are continuous. For $d_1$, let $f_n=1$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$, $f_n=0$ on
$[\tfrac12+\tfrac1n,1]$ and linear in between. Then
$d_1(f_n,f_m)=\tfrac12\left\lvert\tfrac1n-\tfrac1m\right\rvert\to0$, so $\{f_n\}$
is $d_1$-Cauchy, but not $d_\infty$-Cauchy since
$d_\infty(f_n,f_{2n})\geq\tfrac12$. If $f_n\to f$ in $d_1$ with $f$ continuous, then
$f=1$ on $[0,\tfrac12]$ and $f=0$ on $(\tfrac12,1]$, which is not continuous at
$\tfrac12$. So no limit exists in $C([0,1])$.

:::

:::{.definition data-title="Compact Metric Space"}

A metric space $X$ is **(sequentially) compact** if every sequence in $X$ has a
subsequence converging to a point of $X$. A compact metric space is complete and
bounded, and in $\mathbb{R}^n$ the compact sets are exactly the closed and
bounded ones (Heine-Borel). See [[compactness]].

:::
